national.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
national.summary: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
national.body:
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.

The retreat, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.

Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.

He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.

Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.

national.title: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
national.summary: The U.S. birth rate fell to its lowest level ever recorded, according to a report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The drop would have been greater, but women over age 30 are having more children.
national.body:
Fewer women in their 20s are choosing to become mothers, leading to an overall birthrate decline in the U.S. But the birth rate among U.S. women age 30-45 is rising according to the latest federal data. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP hide caption

Sarah Harris was 37 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

News 710,000 fewer babies were born last year in U.S. compared with two decades ago Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

national.summary: The U.S. ambassador to the U.N. says the war with Iran could last another year, but he hopes Tehran will "come to the table" sooner.
national.body: Iran said on Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and President Trump will "take that dream to his grave". The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as U.S. ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weekend. "We will not allow U.S. military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television. "The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave." CBS/AFP

national.title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
national.summary: She was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
national.body:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.

A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.

Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.

All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.

More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.

Kenya's latest victim had been under quarantine when she developed symptoms on 13 October, the health ministry said.

The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.

Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.

national.title: Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
national.summary: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.
national.body:
A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.

national.title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
national.summary: Every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
national.body:
Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.

But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.

Only on NPR The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.

These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

Voting What's behind the early voting surge? It's more than voter enthusiasm, expert says But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.

All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.

national.title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
national.summary: A gunman opened fire from his car in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
national.body: A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated."These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents in the suburb of Trappes, west of Paris. "There is no place for this in France."The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV. "This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, The Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties. Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station. The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger. A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency. Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin." Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims. national.title: Paris museums close, shops build barricades ahead of more protests
national.summary: A week after 3,000 shops were damaged or looted, France braces for more protests.
national.body: Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week's violent unrest that shocked the country.France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais - where a Cézanne exhibit is on display - are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend's hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend. The demonstrations first erupted last month when high school students in southeast of Paris protested for better conditions, but quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election. national.title: White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
national.summary: Ukraine and Russia confirm the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
national.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.

It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.

Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 02:00 GMT on 27 October.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.

The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".

national.title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
national.summary: Taiz, a city in southwestern Yemen, faces a severe water crisis as Houthi rebels backed by Iran tighten their encirclement. The city has struggled with water issues for over a decade, but the situation has worsened in recent weeks.
national.body:
Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.

"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.

Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.

Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

national.title: One arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle Nest mountain retreat
national.summary: Police said firefighting efforts were hampered due to local conditions.
national.body: A suspect has been detained in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and there were no injuries reported. Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added."Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hilter era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

national.title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
national.summary: Greg Bovino was the public face of the controversial immigration enforcement operation in the city earlier this year.
national.body:
The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".

Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".

A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

national.title: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
national.summary: Calls for change present a challenge to President Lula in the second round of the election on Sunday.
national.body:
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.

Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.

"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.

"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

national.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
national.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in a memo to Secretary of State Rubio that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," and the plots have "reached advanced stages."
national.body: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen."The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent. Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.Axios was first to report on the memo.The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported."When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.

The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.

Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.

Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

national.title: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
national.summary: Intense rainfall slammed the Four Corners region late this week. As rivers flooded, towns declared evacuations and emergencies and made rescues.
national.body:
Floodwaters surround trailers at the Fun Valley Family Resort campground and RV part in South Fork, Colo., early Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. South Fork Fire Rescue/AP hide caption

Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."

Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.

"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.

"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."

Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.

Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.

national.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
national.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
national.body:
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.

From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".

Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.

The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".

It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".

"I liked how happy I genuinely looked."However, the response to the video that was posted in March was toxic. "Then like overnight, hundreds of hate comments," Salyars said. "â¦ 'You're really ugly, you're fat, your husband deserves better.' It just kept going."For a full month after, people piled on with hundreds of insults. That is, until the tide turned and a wave of encouragement drowned out the trolls."It was weird because, where are all these really nice people coming from?" Salyars asked. It was such a drastic shift, it really defied explanation. To Kahri Salyars it almost felt like an organized effort, like an army of kindness warriors had just come rushing to her defense. That turned out to be exactly what it was.Tyler Brickley of Kansas City, Missouri, runs "The Kindness Mob," a group about half a million strong that secretly battles internet spite. "We make every effort for them to never find out," Brickley said. First, the Kindness Mob picks a target, someone who is being bullied. Then, they shower that person with compliments.Brickley said the goal is to try and make the internet seem kind. "It feels outrageous, but that's exactly what we're trying to do," Brickley said. "And it's the most beautiful thing I've ever been a part of."Since starting the group in 2023, Brickley and his Kindness Mob have digitally rescued about 400 strangers, like Salyars, who just can't stop reading the comments.Salyars eventually figured out Brickley was behind the shift, but it didn't matter. She says her confidence is back. "I would say so," Salyars said. "Positivity overtook the hate."

national.title: Rollins says USDA is 'full-bore ahead' on Forest Service reorganization
national.summary: The Trump administration wants to move Forest Service headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City, shutter 23 research stations, and close many regional offices and replace them with state offices.
national.body:
Matthew Brown, Associated Press Matthew Brown, Associated Press

BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday that the Trump administration remains "full-bore ahead" with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service and other agencies after a judge blocked the changes last week.

WATCH: U.S. Forest Service cuts raise concerns on protecting public lands and fighting wildfires

The administration wants to move Forest Service headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City, shutter 23 research stations, and close many regional offices and replace them with state offices. It's part of a broader realignment at the Agriculture Department that also would change programs for food and nutrition, rural development and other services.

For now the plan is stalled under court order. But that's already under appeal, and Rollins made clear Thursday that the administration hasn't given up.

"We are full-bore ahead in the reorganization," Rollins said during a conference call with reporters following an announcement on fertilizer production. "We believe in it more today than we ever have — taking the USDA to our constituents, which is rural America, the Forest Service out West."

Administration officials say the reorganization will trim costs and further concentrate resources in Western states that are home to nearly 90% of national forest lands.

Federal employee unions, environmental groups and local officials, including in California, Maryland and Washington state, are trying to quash the plan. They say the shuffling of employees is a ploy to achieve the administration's goal of deep cuts in the workforce.

He said he had decided to go home for lunch that day instead of eating the food he had packed.As he drove by the elementary school, he saw a "man in black" holding a long gun and shooting at a vehicle. At first, he thought it was a prank, but then the shooter threw the gun over the school fence before climbing it."That's when panic fled into my brain and that's when I opened my center console and said, 'No. No. No. No,'" Giamanco said in the interview. In the console of his truck was a .40-caliber handgun he rarely used.He said he grabbed the weapon's magazine from another compartment, drove into the school parking lot and saw the shooter walk across school grounds."I just was in full panic, like, 'No, there's children, there's babies in there,'" he recalled. national.title: Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election
national.summary: Kiryat Shmona, Israel's northernmost city, has long been a bastion of support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party. But that loyalty is no longer ironclad.
national.body:
Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press

KIRYAT SHMONA, Israel (AP) — Kiryat Shmona has long been a bastion of support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party. But that loyalty is no longer ironclad.

Once a bustling commercial center, Israel's northernmost city was temporarily evacuated three years ago after being battered by rockets from nearby Lebanon, and it still feels half-empty even though the attacks have mostly subsided. Although the town remains staunchly conservative, there are rumblings of displeasure with Netanyahu's handling of the latest war against the militant group Hezbollah, and that could bode poorly for him in Israel's election Tuesday.

Vowing to stop Hezbollah's attacks, Netanyahu led a bombing campaign in Lebanon and invaded the country twice since 2023. More than 4,000 Lebanese have been killed, and Israeli troops have occupied a swath of southern Lebanon, leveling multiple towns and displacing an estimated 1 million people.

Still, Hezbollah remains active. Some in Kiryat Shmona say Israel should have been even tougher; others say they no longer trust that Netanyahu cares about them.

Eti Ben Shabat, 64, says in previous elections she had always followed her family in voting for Likud, almost without thinking. But in recent years, she said, something snapped. She pointed in part to Netanyahu's broken promises to bring security to the north and dismantle Hezbollah.

Netanyahu is unlikely to lose Kiryat Shmona entirely. But even a small dip in its support — and that of other traditional strongholds — could spell trouble for him.

It could tip a very tight election to the man aiming to replace him, Gadi Eisenkot. Or it could strengthen far-right parties, which would likely back Netanyahu to remain prime minister but would then have even greater power in a ruling coalition.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other "countries of concern."

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

REAAD MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump's favored term for AI, "superintelligence" or SI.

Friday night was not about what happened before it this season. It was about a rivalry that dates back over 100 years, a trophy to highlight community pride, and bragging rights between the two schools.

For those who root for the home team, Friday was the highlight of their season.

Thanks to two touchdowns apiece from Graham Putney and Ayden Wronski, the Fredonia Hillbillies defeated the Dunkirk Marauders 29-7 in a nonleague rivalry game at the Orange Bowl.

local.body:
FALCONER -- As members of the Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove football team finished their initial celebration after a 43-6 victory over Southwestern/Frewsburg at Bill Race Field on Friday night, they were called together by Drew Wilcox, Falconer's athletic director.

Wilcox handed the ball to the Herd's head coach, Curt Fischer, and another celebration broke out.

The victory made Fischer the winningest head coach in Section VI football history, passing Gene Masters with his 249th career victory.

"Just to have my name mentioned in the same sentence with Coach (Gene) Masters is an honor in itself," Fischer said of the longtime Grand Island and Brocton coach whose record he surpassed. "I was fortunate enough early in my career to watch him and meet him in the stadium games we went to. I have a lot of praise for him and his family."

Fischer's coaching career began at Maple Grove, where he won state titles in 1998 and 2008, before a stint as the coach for a merged Chautauqua Lake/Maple Grove team. He became head coach at Falconer -- his alma mater -- in 2022.

"Coach (Dan) Greco was huge. There are so many people and I don't want to leave a bunch of people out," Fischer said. "All of those players who played for me, I love them all. It was all them. They just worked hard and I was lucky enough to be the head coach."

As the team gathered for a photo, players and other coaches invited Fischer's wife, Lori, and children, Megan and Zach, into the photo.

"They've sacrificed for all of this. My family has sacrificed so much, my wife and kids. They are huge," Curt Fischer said. "They've put up with a lot. I love them all. I can't thank them enough."

local.body:
SILVER CREEK -- For many years, whenever the site of the former Silver Creek School building on Main Street was mentioned at a Village Board meeting, it came with frustration. The site deteriorated for decades and became an eyesore for all who lived in the village.

Now, that site is home to Silver Creek Senior Housing, and with it comes optimism and pride in the village. Park Grove Realty and Southern Tier Environments for Living (STEL) have brought the project to life.

After touring the facility herself, Mayor Kathy Tampio had nothing but good things to say about the new facility as it prepares to open its doors in the coming weeks.

"It is a beautiful facility. They have done a wonderful job," Tampio said, noting the landscaping outside of the facility, as well as architectural aspects including the preservation of the old school sign in the courtyard, in what she called "a special place of prominence."

Silver Creek Senior Housing is a senior community that features 54 one- and two-bedroom apartment homes for individuals and families aged 62 and older. Tampio was told there were 113 applicants for Silver Creek Senior Housing, more than twice as many applicants as there are units.

Because there were more applications than units, a housing lottery will determine who calls Silver Creek Senior Housing their new home. It comes as no surprise that the demand was so high, as the need for affordable senior living has been well documented by community members for many years.

Trustee Sandra Lindstrom recently met with residents from Fredonia who admired the facility. They told her how impressed they were with the project and how much they wished they had a facility like that where they live.

The old Main Street school building was demolished in late spring of 2025. Construction continued all throughout the past year, even through the winter. Now, the facility will be open within weeks. Some of the apartments are nearly finished, with others at various stages of completion.

local.body:
ORCHARD PARK -- Jim Leonhard leaned back to loosen his shoulders and let out a big yawn upon approaching the podium for his weekly news conference before addressing the first question of whether he got any sleep.

“Not much,” the Buffalo Bills’ first-year defensive coordinator said.

The lack of rest was the combination of the team’s late-night return home following a 33-30 win at Las Vegas on Sunday and whatever restlessness Leonhard is experiencing in attempting to plug a leaky defense that’s among the NFL’s worst in yards and points allowed.

Tired as the first-year coordinator felt, the one thing Leonhard wouldn’t give into was frustration.

“Me being frustrated, it doesn’t help us get there,” Leonhard added, while looking ahead to Buffalo entering its bye week off with an AFC East-leading 5-1 record. “It’s going to be a couple of days in the office for us re-evaluating everything. If 75% of the problem is me, then we’ll fix that. But what’s the rest of it that we can clean up for these guys?”

Though pleased with Buffalo’s pass rush, Leonhard conceded his secondary has been a weak spot while allowing 15 touchdown passes, tied for the second most in the NFL entering Week 7. On-field communication continues to be a problem even though Leonhard worked on simplifying the game plan last week.

And then there are disciplinary issues, beyond safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson’s ejection and one-game suspension for spitting in the direction of Raiders players.

A week after allowing the Rams to convert four first downs as a result of penalties in a 37-34 overtime win at LA, five more flags led to Raiders first downs. Overall, the Bills rank last in the NFL with 151 first downs allowed and 21 by penalties. And that has contributed to Buffalo ranking 28th in the league in allowing opponents to convert 45% of their third-down opportunities.

local.body:
Lawrence A. Alexander Sr., known affectionately to many as Tinker, passed away on October 22, 2026, in Brocton, New York, at the age of 75. Born on July 11, 1951, in Jamestown, New York, he lived a life marked by hard work, devotion to family, and a warm presence that will be deeply missed by all who knew him.

Tinker was the son of the late Lawrence and Virginia (Shreve) Alexander. He was also predeceased by his beloved son, Shane Alexander, and by his siblings Mike, Rusty, Ronald, Charlotte, Patricia, and Jerry. He is survived by his companion of 25 years, Mary L. Test, who shared many cherished years by his side. He also leaves behind his children, Lawrence A. Alexander Jr. and his companion, Season, Matthew Alexander, and Marine Alexander Presto, his stepson, Ray (Rachel) Test Jr.(Rachel) along with Eight grandchildren and two great-grandchildren who brought him great pride and joy.

He is further survived by his brother, Dennis Alexander and his wife, Vikki, as well as many nieces, nephews, and cousins who will remember him with love and gratitude. Family was always central to Tinker's life, and he treasured the time he spent with those closest to him. His steady presence, sense of humor, and genuine care for others made him a valued part of his family circle and community.

Tinker made his living as a self-employed contractor in Brocton, New York, where he was known for his strong work ethic, practical skills, and ability to take on just about any project. He took pride in his work and was respected for his reliability and determination. Whether he was helping someone with a job or working on something of his own, he approached each task with the same hands-on spirit that defined so much of his life.

Outside of work, Tinker enjoyed fishing, hunting, and horses, and he was always tinkering with all types of projects. He had a natural curiosity and a talent for fixing, building, and improving things, which earned him his nickname and reflected the way he lived his life. He especially enjoyed spending time with family and friends, and those moments of companionship and laughter were among his most treasured.

local.title: Cardinal Dolan celebrates special Mass at Buffalo's historic St. Stanislaus Church
local.summary: New York City's retired Cardinal Timothy Dolan brought a moment of pride to Buffalo's historic Polonia on the city's East Side, presiding over a special Mass at St. Stanislaus Church.
local.body: New York City's retired Cardinal Timothy Dolan brought a rare moment of pride to Buffalo's historic Polonia on the city's East Side, presiding over a special Mass at St. Stanislaus Church at the invitation of the Polish American Civic Affairs Committee.Before Mass, he greeted community members in the street."My honor to be here," greeted Dolan.The Mass was concelebrated with Catholic Diocese of Buffalo priests.Current Bishop Michael Fisher and former Bishop Richard Malone both took part. Malone resigned as Buffalo's bishop during the height of the clergy abuse scandal. In his sermon, the cardinal called both men his "brothers."I asked Dolan about appearing in Buffalo."I got a beautiful day here in the Diocese of Buffalo, a diocese that I've admired and appreciated for a long time. See my brother bishops and see the great people. You see the marks of the church, the vitality and the pride," Dolan said.Dolan is no stranger to controversy, criticized by abuse survivors for his handling of clergy abuse cases and for his strong, conservative stances on matters of faith. Here’s how he responded."Look, if you get criticism from both sides, you're doing the right thing, right? And I just keep thinking of Pope Saint John Paul II: 'Be not afraid.' Jesus was criticized. He was criticized. I might be part of the gospel. Alright... I better go," Dolan said.For those who came to Mass, the visit was deeply personal."What is the meaning for you to see this prominent figure here?" I asked Amherst resident Dolores Boncal. "It's such an honor, and I feel God called me here today," Boncal said. Republican Chautauqua County Executive P.J. Wendell traveled to Erie County to attend the Mass. He told me this day was bigger than politics."I think we have to look past the politics and look at — you know — you're celebrating the word of God, and that's really transcends it today," Wendell said.Sarah Pickering of Gowanda also attended, agreeing Dolan is controversial.“But the controversy all lies mostly in his backing the traditions of the church, and all of her teachings and not straying when the world would say otherwise," Pickering said.Pickering brought her young son, Timothy Michael, named after the cardinal."My husband and I both have a great love for him. local.title: Buffalo's winter plan faces a hurdle: hiring enough mechanics to keep the plows rolling
local.summary: Buffalo released its annual snow plan, but a mechanic shortage still threatens to keep the city's aging plow fleet off the roads this winter.
local.body: Buffalo has submitted its annual snow plan, but a shortage of mechanics threatens to keep snow plows off the streets when they break down. The city suffered the same problem last winter. Back in February, Buffalo Mayor Sean Ryan revealed the city was down to just 14 working snow plows out of 36. Ryan blamed a combination of factors, including a lack of investment by previous administrations along with struggling to hire enough mechanics to fix the aging fleet."One of the reasons we're down so low is the city stopped properly paying its mechanics," the mayor said at the time.Eight months later, I visited the Broadway Barns to see how the city is preparing for the upcoming winter. I discovered recruiting mechanics is still a problem. There are just 12 mechanics to look after vehicles citywide says Kevin Savage, the city's superintendent of fleet maintenance. "Eight mechanics in this garage, two in police and two in fire," Savage said.Savage remembers when the shop was nearly twice as staffed, estimating there were around 22 mechanics back in 2009 when he first started working at the Broadway Barns. This year, the city has budgeted for close to that number — 20 mechanics. Pay remains a factor in the challenge to fill those positions, according to Deputy Mayor Benjamin Swanekamp. "Our pay's not competitive," Swanekamp said. "We included raises in the budget, but we're still negotiating with the union to try to get them to effectuate those."The average annual salary for an auto mechanic in the Buffalo area is around $53,000, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Nearly half of the city's auto mechanic jobs paid below that under last year's budget. The raises in the Ryan administration's current budget bring the majority of those auto mechanic positions above that salary.Heading into winter understaffed, Savage said his crew is making do."We got a lot of hard-working guys who get the job done every day. We do the best we can with what we have," Savage said.For now, getting to full strength remains the aim for the Ryan administration."Getting fully staffed is a huge goal for us," Swanekamp said.In the meantime, the city has six new snow plows on order to try to mitigate the number of breakdowns. local.title: Radiological investigation in Niagara, Erie counties narrows focus as cleanup planning moves forward
local.summary: State and federal teams have screened more than 1,000 properties, with around 40 referred to the EPA for further investigation. Some cleanup work could begin within weeks.
local.body: State and federal officials say they're narrowing the search for radioactive contamination in Western New York, with cleanup work potentially beginning at some properties in the coming weeks.Since July 23, teams have screened 1,094 properties in Niagara and Erie counties as part of the ongoing investigation. More than 907 property owners have been notified that no additional radiological investigation is needed, according to a new dashboard from the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and the federal Environmental Protection Agency.Forty properties have been referred to the EPA for further investigation. Most are in the Town of Niagara and the City of Niagara Falls, with one in Grand Island. Four properties have received offers of voluntary temporary relocation, while owners of two other parcels declined additional assessment.The next step is more detailed sampling to determine where radioactive material is located, how much is present and what cleanup each property may require.EPA Region 2 Administrator Michael Martucci said some cleanup work could begin within the next couple of weeks. Officials hope to complete work that can be done before winter, while using the colder months to plan more extensive cleanup efforts for spring.Investigators are also conducting what the EPA calls forensic sampling — testing material to compare its characteristics with known historical sources. Officials have not established whether contamination at the various properties shares a common source.The federal government is separately seeking more than $12 million from a company over cleanup costs associated with radioactive waste found beneath two homes on Upper Mountain Road in Lewiston. Martucci said that case is specific to those properties and declined to speculate about any connection to other locations under investigation.Separately, the state is preparing additional environmental investigation at the former Witmer Road Drive-In site in the Town of Niagara, including areas along Gill Creek. Preparatory work will include fencing, signage and brush clearing.DEC Commissioner Amanda Lefton said that investigation is expected to continue into spring 2027.The next community drop-in session is scheduled for Nov. 10 from 4 to 7 p.m. at the Calvin K. local.title: 'A give-back program': Somerset to vote on pensions for volunteer firefighters
local.summary: Neighbors in the Town of Somerset have an extra box to check on Election Day. There is a town proposition about whether to match other areas and provide a paid pension to volunteer firefighters.
local.body: Neighbors in the Town of Somerset have an extra box to check on Election Day. There is a town proposition about whether to match other areas and provide a paid pension to volunteer firefighters.If approved, the proposition would add a Length of Service Award Program (LOSAP) that would give Barker Fire Department firefighters 10 years of monthly pension payments once they turn 65 years old.Firefighters would receive payments of $20 per month for every year of active service (ex., 12-year veteran = $240/month).Qualifying members would need at least five years of active service, and the payments max out at $400/month for 20 years or more of active service.The reason this requires a community vote is that it would be entirely paid for by a special property tax of $0.54 per $1,000 of assessed valuation.“It’s kind of a give-back program for our volunteers taking their time. We spend enough time away from our families,” Barker Fire Department President Stephen Horning said. “On average, they figured [the tax is] going to go up about $50 per household…. but the huge increase of running a full department if we were professionally paid would be astronomical and would not be feasible for the town of Somerset.”“You’re not going to get rich off of it, that’s for sure,” Town Supervisor Jeffrey Dewart said. "But it would be a little bit of an incentive to get new members and keep the ones we have.”WATCH: 'A give-back program': Somerset to vote on pensions for volunteer firefightersWhile not a universal program for departments across the county, fire companies in places such as Lockport, Lewiston and Newfane have already similar payments.This proposition also comes amid a busy year for the Barker Fire Department, as the seemingly ever-expanding Lake Mariner Data Center has increased use of the fire and EMT services.“Several times per week we’ve been there. local.title: Buffalo woman turns breast cancer diagnosis into message of hope
local.summary: October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and a Buffalo woman is sharing her journey with breast cancer to highlight the importance of early detection and knowing your body.
local.body: October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and a Buffalo woman is sharing her journey with breast cancer to highlight the importance of early detection and knowing your body.For Lauren Lee and her husband, life has always revolved around staying active, traveling and exploring new places together. Originally from the Albany area, the couple moved to Buffalo eight years ago and dreamed of visiting every national park in the country.But in May, three months after her 30th birthday, Lee was diagnosed with stage 2 invasive ductal carcinoma, a type of breast cancer.“I found a lump and thought it was suspicious,” Lee said.The diagnosis forced the couple to put travel plans and social lives on hold as they shifted their focus on treatment.“We went from planning, like, park trips and going out with friends and things like that, to then changing all of that to being in an oncologist's office and planning for my next chemo,” Lee said.Lee completed six rounds of chemotherapy over 18 weeks and is preparing for a double mastectomy scheduled for early November.While treatment has been physically and emotionally challenging, Lee said maintaining a positive outlook has helped her through some of her darkest moments.“But being optimistic is everything,” Lee said. “There were some days that I felt so consumed with the diagnosis and depression that came along with it that it was really hard to see the light at the end of the tunnel.”She said completing chemotherapy has given her hope as she prepares for surgery.“The worst is behind me,” she said. “Chemotherapy was terrible, but surgery is next, and that's the next step in getting all of this out.”Lee hopes sharing her experience will encourage other women to prioritize health and advocate for themselves.WATCH: Buffalo woman turns breast cancer diagnosis into message of hopeAccording to the American Cancer Society, about 4% of breast cancer cases in the United States are diagnosed in women younger than 40.“My journey is not unique,” Lee said. “One in eight women will be diagnosed with breast cancer, so screening is super local.summary: It's part of the county's Vision Zero initiative.
local.body:
Monroe County officials have formed a task force to help guide their Vision Zero initiative to eliminate traffic-related deaths and serious injuries.

The task force is made up of representatives from county departments, advocacy groups, city and local governments, elected county officials, advocacy groups, and other community partners.

The members will help the county with efforts such as identifying locations, behaviors, and other factors associated with fatal or serious crashes. The 35-member group also is supposed to help improve collaboration between governments, agencies, and other organizations and work on topics including road design, and best practices to reduce the number and severity of crashes. local.title: Conserve Water Order issued for Fredonia commercial, residential water customers
local.summary: The Village of Fredonia and Chautauqua County Health Department have issued a conserve water order effective Friday, October 23.
local.body: The Village of Fredonia and Chautauqua County Health Department have issued a conserve water order effective Friday, October 23. Seasonal changes in the Fredonia Reservoir water quality are increasingly straining the water treatment plant. As a result, water is moving through the treatment process more slowly, making it difficult for the plant and existing storage reserves to keep pace with normal water demand.The Village is asking all commercial and residential water customers to:• Turn off the faucet while brushing teeth, shaving, or washing dishes.• Thaw frozen foods in the refrigerator or microwave — not under running water.• Take short showers; turn off water while lathering.• Skip pre-rinsing dishes; most dishwashers can remove food particles and stains without pre-rinsing.• Use disposable plates, cups, and utensils.• Only run dishwashers and washing machines with full loads.• Make every toilet flush count. Don’t use the toilet like a garbage can to flush away tissue, etc.• Clean vegetables in a bowl of water, not under the tap.• Do not wash vehicles.• Do not water lawns or landscaping.• Do not hose down sidewalks, decks, or driveways — use a broom instead.• Do not fill pools, hot tubs, or other large containers.• Check for and fix leaks in faucets, toilets, and pipes.For more information, call the Village of Fredonia at (716) 679-2307 or visit their website online here. At 4:49 a.m., Rochester firefighters were dispatched to Pallet Express and when they arrived, they found a fire in the back of the two-story commercial building with flames extending through a hole in the roof, according to a news release from the department.

By 5:21 a.m., crews had the fire under control, according to the release. Firefighters searched the building and found there were no people inside.

local.title: Hochul calls on ICE to release Guillen, Lin
local.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday to release two people arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in western New York.
local.body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul is joining calls seeking the release of two area residents separately detained by federal immigration agents in recent days.

In a statement posted on X , Hochul said she spoke Thursday evening with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the arrests of SUNY Brockport IT technician German Machado Guillen and Mt. Morris restaurant owner Dian Zhao Lin .

"I want their families to know that I'm doing everything in my power to bring their loved one's home," Hochul wrote. "I'm encouraged by the Secretary's willingness to engage, and I'll continue pushing for their swift return."

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents took Guillen into custody last week outside his family home in Batavia. Agents arrested Lin (identified by federal authorities as Sin Di Ling) on Tuesday.

This isn't the first time Hochul has used her position to pressure federal authorities to release individuals detained in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Prior efforts have included college and high school students, as well as a family detained in March 2025 at a Sackets Harbor dairy farm .

ICE, in separate statements, has said both men were here illegally, Guillen having overstayed a visa and Lin having previously been ordered removed by an immigration judge.

U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle, who represents the state's 25th Congressional District, also has lobbied federal authorities for Guillen’s release .

entertainment.summary: The rapper capped a week of festivities with a lavish New York celebration — complete with designer gifts and a $1 million game show.
entertainment.body:
Drake rang in his 40th birthday with more than 400 guests, million-dollar prizes and a surprise performance from the Backstreet Boys — one day after adding another record to his already historic résumé. Explore Drake See latest videos, charts and news

The Toronto superstar celebrated at New York ’s Casa Cipriani on Friday night (Oct. 23), hours before officially turning 40 on Oct. 24. According to TMZ, guests were treated to luxury giveaways including Chanel and Hermès handbags, while a game show held during the party offered cash prizes ranging from tens of thousands of dollars up to $1 million. The night’s biggest musical surprise came courtesy of the Backstreet Boys, who performed for the crowd before Drake joined them onstage for their 1999 hit “ I Want It That Way .”

Amid the spectacle, Drake took a moment to reflect on the milestone.

“Tonight isn’t about a tour, an album release, or a bunch of videos we shot,” he told the room. “It’s about being alive, staying alive.”

The New York celebration capped several days of birthday festivities that began back home in Toronto. Earlier in the week, Drake gathered with friends at the CN Tower, where he was surprised with a collage of photos and memories. Popcaan was among those in attendance.

Drake later traveled to New York with his mother and members of his entourage aboard Air Drake, his customized Boeing 767, and was spotted dining at SoHo restaurant Mamo on Thursday night (Oct. 22).

The Backstreet Boys appearance also carried some history. In July 2022, the group brought Drake onstage during their DNA World Tour stop at Toronto’s Budweiser Stage and introduced him as their “sixth member” before performing “I Want It That Way.”

entertainment.title: Hannah Einbinder Says Speaking Out for Palestine Is “the Bare Minimum”
entertainment.summary: "I know how many eyes I have on me," the 'Hacks' alum adds, explaining why she feels compelled to share her views on political and social issues. "I know that difference that it can make."
entertainment.body:
As she became increasingly well-known during her acclaimed five-season run alongside Jean Smart in HBO Max’s Hacks , Hannah Einbinder has used her time in the spotlight to speak out on various political and social issues she’s passionate about from climate change to AI to, most prominently in recent years, the fate of the Palestinian people amid the Israel -Gaza war.

She famously called for a “free Palestine ” at the end of her 2025 Emmys acceptance speech and was arrested last month , along with other pro-Palestinian Hollywood activists like Susan Sarandon , as part of a protest ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu‘s United Nations address. Related Stories Movies How Pat McAfee Landed His First Acting Role in 'The Mosquito Bowl' -- With Some Help From Bradley Cooper and Tom Cruise News Meghan Markle Says She's Kept Her Children From Her Father "to Protect Them" In Wake of Child Abuse Image Allegations

While some celebs might choose to stay silent about their political views, for Einbinder, there’s no alternative.

“I see it as the bare minimum,” Einbinder said at The New Yorker Festival on Friday of the “responsibility” she feels to speak out about her beliefs. “I think we are living in a time that is perhaps the worst point in human history. I think the threat of AI and climate [change] push us into that territory. And I know how many eyes I have on me. I know that difference that it can make. I know it from a financial perspective. I know that I can raise money. I have done it, and so I know that folks like myself and folks with even larger platforms can make tangible difference in the world. And for me, that’s been very specific to Palestine, and so knowing that, I don’t really see any other option.”

Einbinder, who has previously spoken about how her views on Israel and Palestine have evolved since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, shared more about her recent education and perspective on the Israel-Gaza war at the New Yorker Festival event.

“I started to attend IfNotNow vigils with my friends who were going, who were already anti-Zionists, and I found this amazing Jewish community and these Jewish spaces for me to go on a journey of unlearning the propaganda that we’re fed systemically,” Einbinder told The New Yorker ‘s Rachel Syme. “And once I unlearned all of that, I realized I had to arm myself with a lot of knowledge and really go through, yeah, sort of a relearning period, and when I felt equipped, you know, I started to speak because I think when you see this for what it is, you cannot help — well, some people can, I guess. But I think that it was just so intrinsically tied to my values and my sense of justice, and I felt like I have to make up for lost time because I was complicit and unconscious in this system for so long, and I have to change my mind and I have to learn and grow, and so that’s what I’ve tried to do.”

entertainment.summary: Also this week: Drake finances a new album for a Canadian rapper and Tate McRae's Victoria's Secret performance draws criticism.
entertainment.body:
Billboard Canada has announced some more major global names for Billboard Canada Women In Music, where Cardi B will accept the Global Woman of the Year Award .

Summer Walker will accept the Global Visionary Award. Walker has broken barriers to build a modern global R&B success story based on boundless creativity and radical vulnerability. This year, Walker transformed her now-complete Over It trilogy into her first arena tour , the Finally Still Over It tour, which sold out venues around the world. The tour told the tale of her three albums, kicking off in Toronto and culminating with a special finale in the U.K., with two sold-out nights at London’s O2 Arena.

Celebrating the feat in a special moment captured by Billboard Canada and Billboard UK , Walker paid tribute to the bold and loyal team that has helped her achieve new heights as she has built her own path within the industry.

Bebe Rexha will be honoured with the Global Hitmaker Award , which recognizes her decade-spanning career and illustrious path from songwriter to one of the most versatile charting stars on the music landscape. From pop to electronic, country and R&B, she has shown an ability to craft songs that resonate with massive audiences including multiple No. 1s in Canada and the U.S.

Now in 2026, the singer has taken greater creative control of her career, going independent and partnering with EMPIRE , a decision she describes as not just a business one, but a personal one, “embracing every part” of herself. Her 2026 album Dirty Blonde hit No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Dance Albums chart and reflects Bebe’s newly heightened creative ambition, which includes making music videos for every song on the album.

Chxrry will accept the 2026 Billboard Canada Rising Star Award .

It has been four years since the Scarborough-born, Los Angeles-based act (formerly Chxrry22) made history as the first female artist signed to The Weeknd’s XO record label. Chxrry has continued to build her audience, playing both intimate and stadium-sized concerts during her opening stint on The Weeknd’s record-breaking After Hours Til Dawn tour . This year, she played 16 sold-out shows across the globe, including two stops in Toronto.

The celebration will be hosted by Leandra Earl and Kylie Miller of The Beaches, the breakthrough Toronto band that was recognized as last year’s Women of the Year.

entertainment.body:
Logo text [This story contains spoilers for Street Fighter .]

When Street Fighter star Callina Liang was cast as Chun-Li, one of her all-time favorite video game characters, she understood the fans’ skepticism. In fact, she shared their concerns that her physique didn’t yet match that of the beloved martial artist, whom many consider the most iconic female character in fighting games. She didn’t take the criticism personally, but she still used it as bulletin board material to hopefully win over her doubters.

“A lot of the comments I read online motivated me even more to prove them wrong. But I agree that, physically, where I started wasn’t where I would ideally want Chun-Li to be,” Liang tells The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories Movies 'Street Fighter' Director Kitao Sakurai Built a Career by Embracing the Ridiculous Movies 'You Can See Everything' Triumphs With $15M as 'Street Fighter' Wins Weekend

From that moment on, Liang went all-in on becoming the beloved fighter, putting herself through an intense physical transformation to embody the undercover Interpol agent. She pumped iron multiple times a week, trained in stunts and martial arts daily and followed a rigorous diet that included 12 eggs per day.

For a character whose martial arts style is defined by her powerful kicks, Liang added nearly three inches to her thighs. The physical overhaul was so dramatic that her stunt double had to wear “butt pads” to mirror Liang’s new figure whenever they swapped in and out of scenes. It’s a staggering metamorphosis, particularly for anyone familiar with the Canadian-Chinese actor’s previous roles as high school girls exploited by their classmates in Steven Soderbergh’s Presence and J.C. Lee’s Bad Genius .

“Honestly, I wasn’t expecting [my legs to keep growing], but the amazing crafty table they had on set definitely helped,” Liang says. “I definitely felt the pressure. I just didn’t want to disappoint anyone.”

Chun-Li infiltrates Lord M. Bison’s (David Dastmalchian) criminal and military organization to avenge her father’s murder at the hands of the Shadaloo leader. At the same time, Bison seeks to lure Ryu (Andrew Koji) into his second World Warrior tournament, where he plans to siphon the reigning champion’s psycho power for himself. Chun-Li helps track down Ken Masters’ (Noah Centineo) estranged adoptive brother, further ingratiating herself with Bison until he offers to formally welcome her into Shadaloo.

entertainment.title: Nick Reiner’s Push for Release of Trust Money to Be Decided by Mediator
entertainment.summary: Lawyers for the trust have maintained that Reiner can't access the funds because of the so-called slayer statute, which bars people from receiving an inheritance from those they kill.
entertainment.body:
A deal has been struck between lawyers for Nick Reiner and the trust allowing a mediator to decide whether he can access funds set aside for him by his parents. The mediation could open the door for him to rehire Alan Jackson, who has represented Harvey Weinstein and Karen Read, among others, and withdrew from the case because of Reiner’s financial constraints.

“A criminal defendant has a constitutional right to use money that is lawfully his own to be defended by the lawyer he chooses,” Reiner’s lawyer, Anita Wu, said in a statement. “These issues need to get resolved as quickly as possible.” Related Stories General News Jamie Lee Curtis Leaning on "Love and Service" in Honoring the Late Rob and Michele Reiner: "Every Day With Them Was Activism" Lifestyle Jamie Lee Curtis to Receive Inaugural Award Inspired by Rob and Michele Reiner at Children's Institute Gala; John Mayer to Perform

Reiner has been held in custody without bail since pleading not guilty to the murders in February. He was initially charged with two counts of first-degree murder with special circumstances relating to multiple homicides, meaning the maximum sentence he faces is life without parole. The Los Angeles County district attorney’s office has said it will not seek the death penalty after consulting Reiner’s siblings.

The trust’s fiduciaries have maintained that Reiner is barred from accessing money in the trust, citing California’s so-called slayer statute. The law prohibits people from receiving an inheritance from those they kill.

One issue in the case is whether the statute applies since Reiner hasn’t been convicted. Another is whether the money is already his since half of the funds should’ve been dispersed to him on his 30th birthday in 2023. Under the terms of the irrevocable trust, the other half is to be paid to him when he turns 35.

Money from the trust is currently being used to pay for lawyers on both side of the litigation, including those trying to prevent Reiner from accessing the funds. So far, fiduciaries have paid lawyers more than $250,000, according to court filings. The figure is nearly half of the trust, $558,000, Reiner should’ve received when he turned 30.

“None of that makes any sense, or serves anyone’s interests,” Wu said. The mediation will begin in December.

entertainment.title: Ken Atchity, Producer on ‘Joe Somebody’ and ‘The Meg,’ Dies at 82
entertainment.summary: The author and literary manager also worked on Maggie Gyllenhaal’s ‘Hysteria’ and Angelina Jolie’s ‘Life or Something Like It.’
entertainment.body:
Ken Atchity, an author and professor who became a literary manager and producer on such films as Joe Somebody , Hysteria and The Meg , has died. He was 82.

Atchity died Monday of kidney failure at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, his longtime business and producing partner, Chi-Li Wong, told The Hollywood Reporter .

Atchity also was behind 16 romantic telefilms made under the banner of Shades of Love that were produced for cable and video. They ran in Canada and on HBO/Cinemax in the States and were released internationally by Warner Bros. Related Stories TV Michael Gray, Former Teen Idol and Star of 'Shazam!,' Dies at 75 Movies Tom Skerritt, Star of 'Picket Fences' and 'Alien,' Dies at 93

Atchity produced the shark thriller The Meg (2018) and its sequel, Meg 2: The Trench (2023), both starring Jason Statham. (Jon Turteltaub directed the first installment, Ben Wheatley the second.)

In addition to Joe Somebody (2001), starring Tim Allen, and Hysteria (2011), starring Maggie Gyllenhaal, Atchity produced features including Life or Something Like It (2002), starring Angelina Jolie, and Gospel Hill (2008), directed by Giancarlo Esposito.

Other producing credits included the 1989 telefilm The Amityville Horror: The Evil Escapes and the 2010 documentary The Kennedy Detail .

An author of more than 20 books, Atchity headed Story Merchant Books, selling his clients’ work to publishers and to film and television outlets while publishing many other works himself.

One of five kids, Kenneth John Atchity was born on Jan. 16, 1944, in Eunice, Louisiana. Raised in Kansas City, Missouri, he graduated from Rockhurst High School with an Ignatian Scholarship to study at Georgetown University (while in high school, he published his first book reviews for The Kansas City Star ).

entertainment.title: Marysa Maslansky, Founder of the Renowned Visages Photo Agency, Dies at 82
entertainment.summary: Her clients included Herb Ritts, Mary Ellen Mark, George Hurrell, Paul Jasmin and William Claxton.
entertainment.body:
Marysa Maslansky, whose influential Visages Photo Agency represented such A-list photographers as Herb Ritts, Mary Ellen Mark and George Hurrell in the 1980s and ’90s, has died. She was 82.

Maslansky died Oct. 9 at her home in Los Angeles after a long illness, a family spokesperson announced.

Born in Pas-de-Calais, France, on April 27, 1944, Maslansky settled in Los Angeles in 1969 and worked as a journalist for the Sygma Photo News agency before heading Gamma Liaison, the L.A. branch of Gamma, the prominent French photo agency. Related Stories TV Michael Gray, Former Teen Idol and Star of 'Shazam!,' Dies at 75 Movies Tom Skerritt, Star of 'Picket Fences' and 'Alien,' Dies at 93

In 1980, she founded Visages, and in addition to Ritts, Mark and Hurrell, the agency would become home to many other iconic celebrity and fashion photographers, among them William Claxton, Greg Gorman, Matthew Rolston, Paul Jasmin, Sofia Coppola, Brad Branson and Firooz Zahedi.

When Ritts started with Maslansky at Visages, his fee was in the range of $750 a day, the Los Angeles Times wrote back then. But by 1990, he was earning about $20,000 a day as one of the highest-paid commercial photographers in the U.S. at the time.

Maslansky was married to Michael Maslansky — a founding partner (with Pat Kingsley and Neil Koenigsberg) of what would become PMK Public Relations — from 1975 until his death in 1993 of stroke complications at age 55. His clients included Goldie Hawn, Sylvester Stallone, Liza Minnelli and Katharine Hepburn .

Survivors include her second husband, Christopher, son Max and daughter-in-law Nancy. Another son, Alex, died in 2023 at age 43.
